title: Would you be ok with making 0$?
author: klas-klattermus
selftext:
Tl;Dr: would you be ok with making 0$ or little money from the games you make? And do you already have a job that lets you live comfortably?

I'm messing around a bit with game dev AI and have completed a couple of simple games, and it was pretty fun! I never tried monetizing, mostly because I fall into the category of people who likes "crazy" ideas and already have an income that lets me and my family live at a lower-middle class standard.

Given the amount of awesome prototypes that I've seen and also amount of games I see being released, obviously we will have more people expressing themselves through games and also more competition for commercial products. What I wonder however, is how many of you guys do it for the love of the game and who here is looking for financial freedom or maybe fame and attention?

Can we have a little discussion about your expectations of AI game dev?

comments.author: phira
comments.body: I don't expect to make any money off it. Let's face it, I'm spending money not making it. It's fun tho, I'm having a blast and learning and making things I love to play

replies.author: jildos_legoplanet
replies.body: Exactly this. I’m learning every day while having fun. That’s what a hobby is, and hobbies usually cost some $

replies.author: Felfedezni
replies.body: Average hobby in America runs around 100-200 a month. So a 20x plan fits within that category.

replies.author: pspahn
replies.body: I expect to make nothing. I use this hobby to learn new dev paradigms, and right now there's clearly _that_ going on, and it helps me stay relevant.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Same here, it's an expensive hobby but not as expensive as Warhammer or MTG :D

comments.author: account009988
comments.body: No

comments.author: DoctorBrandonLau
comments.body: Depends on how much effort I put in/and how good the results are

comments.author: LudwigLoewenlunte
comments.body:
yes have a job. just doing it for fun and because i want to play what i make and it does not exist yet. also exploring cross marketing, mobile etc. it is just pure (expensive) fun. 

for everything i have i invested 230$ and currently made 0 - but nothing is out yet

comments.author: Will_X_Intent
comments.body:
My goal is to have some people genuinely enjoy what I build.  Dream goal is to change their lives.  Money?  Only exists to allow me to keep seeking that dream.  

When AI makes money obsolete, I'll be making games.

comments.author: anon999387
comments.body: The choice will be made for you shortly because the barrier to entry to gamedev will soon be so negligible that the "value" of games will crater. There will be great pushback on the concept of a $70 game once they are made in an automated fashion with little human effort or time expended.

replies.author: Torschlusspaniker
replies.body:
Agreed. 

It is like the The Interstellar Paradox. 

Everyone today is building with the slowest and worst tools there will ever be. In a years time all the work and time you put into your tool will be just be a few prompts eclipsing what you did within minutes. 

I was smacked in the head with that fact again today. I have been working on a wifi tool for months that is like unifi designer crossed with pascal editor and I have seen 3 projects already that beat me on graphics and unifi just replicated all but 3 of my networking features within weeks of their last release. (Take a look at [https://dgreenheck.github.io/tidewater/](https://dgreenheck.github.io/tidewater/) , he did it in no time at all)

I made a lot of choices on how the app works but from when I started to now but today's AI could have made many of those choices and leap frog all the work I did in the past.

It hit me that there is no long term monetary value in any tool now.

replies.author: dont-pull-a-druckman
replies.body:
It makes me very excited, but seeing everything I loved to do become so instantly automated... I'm not quite sure how to feel. I love the speed in which I can create things, but I can't help but feel like that line from the Incredibles:

"And when everyone's super....  
no one will be...."

comments.author: Relevant-Positive-48
comments.body:
Before AI coding was a thing, I released 4 indie games in addition to trying and failing to build more than a dozen others over multiple decades.  I made a total of $130 USD on them.

I'm inspired by every success story out there and you might be one but I promise you my story is far more common than the Undertales and Stardew Valleys out there.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Oh yes, being a developer and being a businessperson are definitely a small spot on the Venn diagram

comments.author: takshit2
comments.body: This is like a new expensive hobby now. Rather than buying games, I spend money building games I love playing lol

replies.author: artuuR2
replies.body: You get all excited to have it finished to play it for about 60% of the development, and then you find it's not interesting anymore and start a new one lol.

replies.author: takshit2
replies.body: That is true. Lol we enjoy building more than actually playing it 🤣

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body:
Which is totally ok!
I remember some 20?-ish years ago when I got Minecraft. I got bored after a day but I kept building mods for it for a long time and had a blast

comments.author: Plane_Friend24
comments.body:
yes. 

I even believe artists are mostly overpaid. People message me trying to get commision for one piece of work that will cost the same as an asset bundle pack i can get anywhere else that will include someone elses 20 years of experience bundled into 1.  the people who have been in it for this many years can afford competitive pricing that the newbies will never beat and now with ai, people are getting better at making their own art...   so now even the vets are having issues. 

I also experienced this when smart phones first came out. I was one of the first devs in the playstore and it was great for a time. now there is 100 apps of every possible idea.   your competiting in an endless ocean of oversaturated app of every niche.   Same thing with web dev. The united states may only have 350 million people but the entire world has many many billions more.   In the online world anyone can charge for anything and at any price. you just cant beat the competitive pricing market.   And now even the competition by numbers are going to be exagerated even more in web design because of how easy it is for anyone to make their own website for a few dollars without having to pay a professional web dev who was promised thousands per website when they attenteded their 2008 web course bootcamp.  

  
being comfortable with making $0 is all about accepting the reality of things, accept the competition, accept the market.  The market is always evolving, every few years something new comes out that people can capitlize on if they want but over time, the competition just gets too much.  Take the game runescape for example. Its easier to grind out your highest gp per hour method and buy an expensive skill than it is to train that skill using cheap methods.   you can achieve the same goal in 100 hours or 1,000 hours.    so if we applied that to life, wouldnt it just be easier to secure a steady paycheck/job. then do ai game dev as a hobby, if it makes you money great, but if it doesnt, at least your bills are paid and you dont have to get depression over it. especially when you zoom out and look around and outside your own bias and bubble , it all feels a bit silly to get upset over.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Yeah, it would be great if we could make a more fair world so people wouldn't feel a need to make apps and games to make money

replies.author: Plane_Friend24
replies.body: yea that would be nice.

replies.author: Danilo_____
replies.body:
As a commercial artist, who makes a living producing art, one asset from me would cost you the price of at least 10 asset pack. Not one.

Glad that you are not my client

replies.author: Plane_Friend24
replies.body: uhuh..... well im glad you are making a living.  Notice how I dont have to be as rude to you as you are to me? I must have hit a chord, unless you are normally this hostile to everyone you meet.

replies.author: Danilo_____
replies.body:
Artists in general have to take a lot of bullshit, like "artists are overpriced" and its worst now with AI. This not ego, this is positioning and this is what makes me money in this economy.   
I am a very humble person but sometimes, you need to be rude with internet bullshit to make a point.

Asset packs are very cheap and it makes sense that they are cheap because they are not exclusive and they make money in volume sells. So, an artist that charges the same price as a asset pack for custom work is charging very cheap and its in the wrong market serving the wrong clients. 

And this is your price comparison? I know for sure that you never worked as an artist or as a freelance for advertising, movies or games. You are a curious person, tickling with AI and making wrong conclusions about things that you doesn't understand. Your take is a ignorant take. Sorry

replies.author: Plane_Friend24
replies.body:
While I do think artists in general take alot of bullshit.  I do not think I am wrong.  Your experience is unique to you.    I dont think you speak for all artists.   You are correct that I am not an artist.  I am not a game designer either. I write backend systems that usually do not require any artwork at all. My software work is more about math and charts and excel sheets than anything else. very boring and uncreative stuff and i admit that is one of my weakpoints... and  You are right that I am dabbling in ai game dev  as a newbie.   But in my opinion I think every take is fair.  

positioning only works if other people interpret your positioning the way you intend it.   Its not a very good business sense in my opinion to set yourself up in a bubble of your own experiences.  I had an experience, I spent money, etc.   You had an experience and you made money etc. Both are fair takes and both can be true to varying degrees.  im sure when the right questions are asked, your opinion would hold alot of weight.  although how you applied that positioning feels a little shortsighted.  I merely tried to explain a pattern I observed with how the difficulty in making money, in fields of creation,  scales over time. i never meant to belittle anyone or claim that its possible. just highlight that i think its difficult.  



 I am happy you are doing opposite of the stereo type of the difficulty of success most artists seem to have.    From the outside looking in, I think most people sympathize with how difficult it is for artists because of how difficult it can be to earn those commissions. I am happy that you specifically are getting high paying comissions that can afford your bills and lifestyle. I am happy for you. truely. I just do not believe that is true for most artists.   If you want to position yourself as some sort of skilled expert, all the more power to you, but then how  would that apply to most artists which are struggling. Your take would be in the minority of experiences of most artists. do you get it?  Your take is the ignorant one because your likely a victim of your own success which is not necessarily bad. but there is a reason why the word bias exists.   An open mind accepts there is more than one take.  I dont have to be a professional artist to be part of the ecosystem that is made of both buyers and sellers.  because lets not forget the original topic of this post .. wether people here are okay with making no money.     you not struggling and calling other artists(your competition) trash. does not really contribute much to the conversation.   maybe I am cheap , maybe others here are too. but I do know often in game development that graphics can go through multiple iterations before release.   you not wanting me as a customer is short sited too. that outburst is weird. other people are reading this you know.  They might want to upgrade their graphics if they become satisfied enough with their game and want to hire a real artist, like you, to perfect the job.     Releasing prototypes and betas is part of the game development process. im surprised an artist like you does not realize that.   every cheapskate here who buys bad artwork has a higher potential to become your next customer than the average joe.

replies.author: Odd_Style_9920
replies.body: Dont even waste time here. Those people think their AI game will ever make money when whole gaming community is against it and they will get flagged right when they get published. Let them dream about making AI ''art'' cause its just funny.

replies.author: Danilo_____
replies.body:
Yes... and I am not even against AI. I use it as a tool at work, as everybody else. But I don't worship this thing as some people who belive that AI are really capable to create artistic work. They are capable to answer, to generate, and to simulate artistic creation and this is usefull. 

I believe that someday we will have a fully AI game that will gain mass appeal. Why not? By lucky AI can generate something that works and with some lucky it will sell it a lot. This is not impossible and is not years ahead. But guess what? Even Flappy Bird (a generic as hell game) made a lot of money in the past.

But this is diferent than "game dev is over" and different than "Everybody will play one prompt AI games"

comments.author: JohnSnowHenry
comments.body:
Yes and yes.

I make games as an hobbie. Not expecting to get money, for that there are hundreds of better jobs to focus your time on

comments.author: EpicOfBrave
comments.body:
Yes, this lesson is very important.

Don’t live in a delusion you will become millionaire by making a software app.

comments.author: JCBAwesomist
comments.body: Would love to be able to quit my job and work full time on making games but I'm not optimistic.

comments.author: Felfedezni

comments.author: Ball_Analytics
comments.body: I wouldn’t mind a $ but it’s a passion project, Im no longer comfortable by any means though at least I have time for this.

comments.author: ByteBandit_45
comments.body:
My plan is to make my wave shooter (like cod zombies but not with zombies enemies) free to play. Its way more worth for me if my game is played instead earning $10 with it. 

So my reward is build a community instead making money. Can be done with second release if my plan works out.

comments.author: MotivatedforGames
comments.body: My goal is to receive feedback and recoup all costs. Turning a profit would be amazing but my main ordeal is ensuring I get big enough consensus as well as financial recoupments.

comments.author: RickRelentless

If you only make games to make money you are so much better off doing pretty much anything else. You’d make more per hour working at a bar or literally doing door dash or uber then 95% of video games make.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Amen, same goes for most app development I bet

comments.author: Itchy-Individual3536
comments.body: Absolutely. I've enjoyed a lot of free and open source games, and as long as I have no cost (or at least no running costs, or not more than I can write off as investing in a hobby or investing in learning) I'm happy when others enjoy what I made.

comments.author: AxiosXiphos
comments.body: I only make games for me. Much much less stressful, and I can do what I want when I want as much as I want.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: My friend donated to my [game](https://vibecodedgames.itch.io/pavement). And I'm still spending more on A.I. than I'm making.

comments.author: Calm-Shirt214
comments.body: Yes, its ok for me. I love building articial lego.

comments.author: siberianmi
comments.body:
My expectations are zero dollars, I’m here for the fun of creating things and seeing how far I can push the models.

My day to day job pays me more than enough this just fun for me and an interesting way to spend some time.

comments.author: AlgaeNo3373
comments.body:
Living comfortably and so is my cat so I don't need to be some breakout viral success to put food on table or feel validated.   
  
I do this as a hobby and enjoy it as such! I used to work in games industry, so for me it's like returning to a discipline I hadn't thought much about for a decade, and seeing that I can do things that previously in the studio I worked for took whole teams. 

People say "AGI" is some vague term and I am confused bc I always thought it meant something around "generally able to replace most economically valuable human labour" and while we are mercifully not at that point yet, if you are old like me, worked in game studio like me, you can see there is a pretty dramatic change already well underway. 

I personally love it, and feel very encouraged by it. I think game-making is an ancient and deeply human form of storytelling. The more hoomans that are able to tell their stories and make their ideas into shareable tangible realities, the better off I think human culture is. 

So my "expectation" if we're gonna throw that around is more cultural-level not individual, and about what it can do for us as a global village when storytelling gets easier and easier. Sharing, already, was what the internet gave us. Creating is what comes next perhaps. I like to be optimistic about this aspect.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body:
Yeah, the spirit of ye olde internet was beautiful, sharing is caring!
The only problem is that the people controlling the technology are also in too much control of government, so the question is what happens if another 10 or 20% of the workforce end up unemployed. I can of course always get a different job, but having already done a handful of different non-tech jobs I know that the pay and working conditions are severely lacking in many sectors and its not going to improve with more competition between workers.

comments.author: Schnitzhole
comments.body:
I do it for the love of the game but I would be fine making net $0 if it covers the cost of listing the game and all that.

Even steam charges $100 to list your free game and app stores even more.

comments.author: mahrogamers
comments.body: I think it all comes down to having something inside you that you genuinely want to create first. Once you achieve that, you naturally hope it can make you some money too

comments.author: bombero_kmn
comments.body:
Im not only OK with it, it's the way i want it. 

I grew up on shareware, freeware, and FOSS in the 90s. It was a formative time that really encouraged my curiosity and love of computers in general. Being able to put something back into that ecosystem feels good.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body:
Heck yes, from sharing cassette tapes and floppies in the schoolyard to flexing whose parents are rich enough to give you the swaggiest skins in Fortnite and Roblox is a huge step back in humanity's development.
If anything I'd love to see us be able to create and share things cheaper and more freely

comments.author: MattMaxBuilds
comments.body: I’d rather have communities built around my games than make money from them. If I wanted to optimize for money, I’d just clone popular games or formats. That brings me no joy. I do it for the love of the game.

comments.author: HurryOne
comments.body: ![gif](giphy|DOPKHQg6oFWUg)

comments.author: Odd_Style_9920
comments.body: You will not make money from AI game anytime soon. Your biggest place to sell it is steam and they will flag you for it pretty fast. If you are not on steam then you dont exist.

comments.author: geddy
comments.body:
\> Can we have a little discussion about your expectations of AI game dev?

Well, for me it's a hobby where I can create the little games I always wanted to play, and in most cases they actually weren't that great. Now I don't have to always wonder "should I try to learn how to make games and spend every night for months staring at code for something that may possibly suck". I am a software engineer by the way, just not a game developer. Not having to spend even more of my life writing code is amazing, particularly when it's for fun little things like this.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Totally agree, the most interesting parts are never memorizing the functions of a framework to learn how to accomplish your goal

comments.author: isaktech
comments.body: I wish I was at $0! After various expenses for hosting my sudoku games puzzle generation infra, and Claude code, and web server for a page, advertising spend… it adds up!

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Hah, yeah! Maybe it would be a good idea to rent some community servers to lower the costs

replies.author: isaktech
replies.body: Where would you rent from? I’m down to try anything to lower costs haha

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body:
I mean that's a separate problem in itself... I'm boycotting US tech until we know if Trump plans to blow us up so that makes things both more expensive and harder to use globally.
But really you could probably get the cost down to a couple of $/€ per month per game

comments.author: Wainfare
comments.body:
Pretty much the same as you tbh. I've got a day job so this is just a hobby for me. if I ever make a bit of money from it, great, but I'm not counting on it

for me the fun bit is actually being able to make stuff. I can't code, so a few years ago none of this would have happened. now I can knock something together over a few evenings and see if it works, which is kind of mad

agree there's going to be loads more competition, but I think getting people to actually find your game is the hard part now, not making it. so if money's the main goal I reckon a lot of people are going to be disappointed

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body:
Yeah and it's also the worse thing, just look at mobile games, you need to force dirty advertising up people's arses to get traction and almost every top game is a variation of the same handful of concepts.
The people with an advertising budget wins, with the exception of a few viral unicorns

comments.author: meshifthenelse
comments.body: I'd rather live under a bridge and barbecue my own poop, than sell my games for anything above 0$

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Is your heart that big or your games that bad?

replies.author: meshifthenelse
replies.body: I just think it's a luxury to have a hobby that costs 200$ a month which many of us don't have.

replies.author: klas-klattermus
replies.body: Yeah but then again that's what some people spend on drinks on a Saturday so c'est la vie!

comments.author: CraftyWitchInc
comments.body: I'm just glad that I can tell the stories I want to in a way that I hope others will also enjoy. I'm disabled so AI allows me to do what I'm good at without being overwhelmed by the things I struggled and repeatedly failed to learn

comments.author: SweetTeaSerums
comments.body: Ok so I'm one of those people! I spend a lot of spare time building stuff just for fun. My brain's always creating, and it's fine if I don't make a dime on these side projects. It makes me happy and gives me a hobby. My kids are getting older now, so they don't need mom and dad as much. I've spent the past month building a "cozy game" called the Virtual Dollhouse Club (posted online if you're curious). It's been so much fun!  I'm definitely not in it for the money.. I do it to have a creative outlet! But hey, if I can get some subscribers that’d be awesome. I’m super proud of it, but if nothing happens I’ll be fine. I’ve got a full‑time gig otherwise.  My advice.. Just keep going and be brave enough to put yourself out there. You never know what might happen!  I think an AI game is fine as long as you don’t just one‑shot it and actually put time and effort into making it the best it can be. It’s gotta be a reflection of your taste and judgement at the end of the day, something you crafted that no one else with the same tools and technology could ever do.
